opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift was in mindset more than any single technical trick. With the first generation, we largely took a model that was designed for vision or language, something that had learned a lot from internet data, and then tried to adapt it to control a robot. That works to a degree, but you quickly feel the mismatch. Those models are very good at describing the world. They're not necessarily good at acting in it.

So for the second generation, the question we asked was: if the end goal is a body interacting with the physical world, what should the model actually be paying attention to? A few things changed as a result.

First, the representation. For embodiment you care much more about geometry, contact, and dynamics: where exactly an object is, how it will move if you push it, whether the gripper is about to slip. A purely semantic understanding of "there's a cup on the table" isn't enough. We put a lot more emphasis on spatial and temporal understanding, so the model builds a sense of 3D structure and of how things evolve over time, rather than just recognizing categories in a single frame.

Second, the action side. In the earlier design, actions were almost an afterthought, a small head attached to a big perception backbone. Now we treat action as a first-class modality. The model has to output smooth, continuous, physically plausible motion at a fairly high frequency, and that changes how you structure the architecture and the training objectives. We also found that letting the model reason about future states, essentially imagining what happens next, makes the actions much more robust.

Third, the data. Internet data is huge, but very little of it is from the robot's point of view, with proprioception and force and the consequences of its own actions. So we designed the model to use a mix: large-scale video for general world knowledge, simulation for scale and diversity, and real robot data for grounding. The architecture was built so those sources complement each other instead of fighting each other.

The improvements show up most clearly in generalization. With the first generation, a new object, new lighting, or a slightly different table height could cause a failure. The second generation degrades much more gracefully. It's not perfect, and long-horizon tasks and fine dexterous manipulation are still hard, but it behaves less like a demo that works under controlled conditions and more like something starting to understand the physical world it's operating in. For me that's the real meaning of designing for embodiment: the body isn't an output device bolted onto an intelligent model. It shapes what intelligence needs to be.

r001.rationale: The response says the second-generation model generalizes better to new objects, lighting, and table heights, and degrades more gracefully in those changed conditions.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a ball-return demonstration or state that visual sensing relies exclusively on onboard cameras.

r003.rationale: It mentions high-frequency motion output, but does not say that returning a ball during fast exchanges requires very little delay.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The biggest shift from the first generation to the second was that we stopped treating the model as something you bolt onto a robot, and started treating the robot as the thing the model is for. With the first generation, we were essentially taking a vision-language backbone, freezing a lot of it, and training an action head on top. That works for demos, but the backbone never really "knew" it had a body. It understood images and text, but it had no native sense of its own joint limits, its own camera placement, or how its actions would change what it sees next.

So the first improvement is in the perception side. Instead of feeding single frames into a model that was pretrained on internet photos, we designed the input to be inherently multi-view and temporal, tied to where the cameras actually sit on the robot. The model learns a consistent spatial representation of the workspace, so when the arm occludes something, it doesn't lose track of it. That alone cut a huge class of failures we used to see in grasping.

The second is on the action side. We moved away from predicting one action at a time and toward predicting short trajectories with a representation that respects the kinematics of the body. When the action space is designed around the embodiment, the model's errors become smoother and more recoverable. It stops producing physically implausible commands that the controller then has to fight.

The third, and honestly the one I care most about, is the data loop. Once the architecture is designed for the body, the robot's own experience becomes high-quality training data, because there's no mismatch between what it collected and what the model consumes. In the first generation, we were constantly converting between formats and losing information. Now failures in deployment flow back almost directly into training, and we see the improvement in the next version within days rather than months.

The honest tradeoff is generality. A model built for a specific embodiment is harder to transfer to a very different robot. We're trying to address that by factoring out the body-specific parts, but I'd rather have a system that works reliably on one body today than one that works mediocrely on ten.

r001.rationale: It describes retaining track of objects when the arm occludes them and making action errors smoother and more recoverable, showing improved handling of unexpected conditions.

r002.rationale: It mentions robot-mounted cameras, but does not describe a ball-return demonstration or say that visual sensing relies exclusively on onboard cameras.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss returning a ball in fast exchanges or the need for very low response delay.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest improvement is that we can design perception, reasoning, and action together. For a robot, understanding a scene is only part of the problem. It also needs to understand what its body can do, what might happen when it moves, and how to adjust based on feedback.

So designing the model specifically for embodiment means treating that interaction as central. If the robot reaches for something and the object moves, it needs to update its action continuously. It can’t simply produce a plan and assume the world will follow it.

That’s where I would expect the main gains: better coordination between perception and movement, more consistent execution, and better recovery when something unexpected happens. Ultimately, the measure is whether the robot can complete a task reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says expected gains include better recovery when something unexpected happens, clearly communicating improved handling of unpredictable situations.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe fast exchanges with a person or the need to respond with very little delay.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest improvement is that we’re designing the model around the whole perception-to-action loop. A robot needs to understand what’s happening, decide what to do, and respond to the results of its own actions. Those capabilities have to work together.

For the second generation, that means making physical interaction central to the model’s design: how observations connect to actions, how the robot uses feedback, and how it adjusts when something doesn’t go as expected. The goal is more reliable execution and better adaptation to different situations. We’d ultimately judge the improvement by whether the robot can complete tasks consistently in the real world.

r001.rationale: It says the model uses feedback to adjust when things do not go as expected, improving adaptation to different situations.
